prompt: A class in a class diagram is a rectangle with how many compartments, holding what?

options.text: Two: name and attributes
Three: name at the top, attributes in the middle, operations at the bottom
Three: attributes, name, operations
Four: name, attributes, operations, relationships

explanation: Three compartments: name, attributes, operations, top to bottom.

why.a: Wrong. Operations have their own compartment.
why.c: Wrong. The name is at the top.
why.d: Wrong. Relationships are lines between classes, not a compartment.

prompt: Match each class relationship with the course text's example or symbol.

pairs.right: One Student with many Enrolment records, labelled with multiplicity
A Department has Lecturers, who can move and still exist
An Order and its Order Lines, deleted together
A hollow triangle pointing to the superclass

explanation: Association is a general link; aggregation is whole-part where the part survives; composition is whole-part where it does not; inheritance points a hollow triangle at the superclass.

prompt: What is the difference between aggregation and composition?

options.text: In aggregation the part CAN exist without the whole; in composition it CANNOT
In composition the part can exist without the whole; in aggregation it cannot
Aggregation is between actors; composition is between use cases
There is no difference

explanation: Composition is the STRONGER form. A lecturer outlives a department move (aggregation); an order line dies with its order (composition).

why.c: Wrong. Both are relationships between classes.
why.d: Wrong. The text draws a clear difference.

prompt: True or false: an Order and its Order Lines are the course text's example of composition, because deleting the order deletes its order lines too.
explanation: The part cannot exist without the whole: composition.

why.false: Wrong. This is exactly the example given.

prompt: How is inheritance drawn in a class diagram?

options.text: A line with a hollow triangle pointing to the superclass
A dashed arrow labelled include
A diamond labelled with a verb
Two parallel lines

explanation: A hollow triangle at the superclass end; the subclass inherits its attributes and operations.

why.a: Correct. Hollow triangle to the superclass.
why.b: Wrong. That is an include relationship between use cases.
why.c: Wrong. That is an ERD relationship.
why.d: Wrong. That is a DFD data store.

prompt: True or false: the four class relationships look similar because a line is a line; the small symbol at one end is what tells them apart.
explanation: Read the END of the line: plain, hollow diamond, filled diamond, or hollow triangle.

why.true: Correct. The symbol at the end decides.
why.false: Wrong. The text says exactly this.

prompt: What is the LAST of the five steps to build a class diagram?

options.text: Identify the candidate classes
Identify the operations of each class
Check that the classes are consistent with the use cases already produced
Identify the relationships and multiplicity

explanation: Candidate classes; relationships and multiplicity; attributes; operations; then CHECK against the use cases.

why.a: Wrong. That is the first step.
why.c: Correct. The consistency check closes the process.

prompt: In the course text's worked class diagram, which class is the ASSOCIATIVE class, and why is it needed?

options.text: Student, because every course needs one
Enrolment, because a student registers for many courses and a course has many students
Course, because it holds the grade
Lecturer, because lecturers teach many courses

explanation: Enrolment resolves the many-to-many between Student and Course, just as an associative entity does in an ERD.

why.a: Wrong. Student is a main class.
why.c: Wrong. Course is a main class.
why.d: Wrong. Not in the worked example.

prompt: True or false: although introduced in requirements modelling, use case diagrams are also considered a UML behavioural diagram.
explanation: They show how external agents interact with the system, which is behaviour.

why.false: Wrong. The text places them among behavioural diagrams.

prompt: Match each example with the use case relationship it shows.

pairs.left: Record Grades always ends with Save Grades
Apply Discount runs only when a discount code is entered
A teacher is connected by a line to Record Grades

explanation: Include is ALWAYS; extend is SOMETIMES, under a condition; association joins an actor to a use case.

prompt: Include and extend are both drawn as dashed arrows. What does the course text say distinguishes them?

options.text: The colour of the arrow
The direction of the arrow, and the meaning of ALWAYS against SOMETIMES
Include uses a triangle and extend a diamond
Nothing; they are interchangeable

why.a: Wrong. Colour is not the distinction.
why.b: Correct. Direction and always against sometimes.

prompt: True or false: EXTEND means a base use case always requires the other use case's behaviour to complete.
explanation: That is INCLUDE. Extend OPTIONALLY adds behaviour under certain conditions.

prompt: Which is the correct order of the four steps to build a use case diagram?

options.text: Actors; use cases; association lines; include and extend relationships
Include and extend; actors; use cases; association lines
Use cases; include and extend; actors; lines
Classes; attributes; operations; check

explanation: Identify the actors; identify their use cases; draw association lines; then add include or extend relationships as labelled dashed arrows.

why.a: Correct. The four steps in order.
why.b: Wrong. Relationships between use cases come last.
why.d: Wrong. Those are class diagram steps.

prompt: In the course text's school grading use case example, which two are ACTORS?

options.text: Teacher
Record Grades
Administrator
Save/Load Grades

explanation: The actors are Teacher, Administrator and Student. Record Grades, Update Grades, Distribute Report Cards, Generate Report Cards and View Grades are use cases, and Save/Load Grades is included by two of them.

why.b: Wrong. Record Grades is a use case.
why.d: Wrong. Save/Load Grades is an included use case.

prompt: True or false: an association line in a class diagram is often labelled with the multiplicity, such as 1 or M.
explanation: Multiplicity, as in one Student associated with many Enrolment records.

why.false: Wrong. The text says associations carry multiplicity.

prompt: What does a class diagram depict?

options.text: The object structure of a system: classes, attributes, operations and relationships
The order of messages over time
Where each part of the system physically runs
The flow of data between processes

explanation: Structure: the classes with their attributes and operations and how they relate.

why.b: Wrong. That is a sequence diagram.
why.c: Wrong. That is a deployment diagram.
